newsitem.title: NICARAGUA: Nicaragua's Chamorro seeks to quell protest.
newsitem.headline: Nicaragua's Chamorro seeks to quell protest.

text.p: The left-wing Sandinista Front's call for "a day of civic protest" on Friday to protest against alleged fraud in the Oct. 20 presidential elections has Nicaraguans divided and nervous, President Violeta Chamorro said.
"I strongly disagree with calling the people to protest. We should promote peace and reconciliation -- and know how to lose," Chamorro, who leaves office on Jan. 10, told reporters late on Tuesday.
State-owned Radio Nicaragua repeated Chamorro's message several times on Wednesday.

Some see the Sandinista protest as potential chaos, remembering Chamorro's nearly seven years in office, when powerful Sandinista activists sometimes paralysed the country, testing a fledgling democracy and shaky political stability.

But for the Sandinistas, attempting to regain power lost when Chamorro routed them in a surprising 1990 election, it is a protest against this year's elections, apparently won by archrival Arnoldo Aleman of the right-wing Liberal Alliance.

The protest, called for Nov. 8 to mark the anniversary of the death of Sandinista Front founder Carlos Fonseca Amador, is part of a broader campaign against the vote's preliminary results. They have Aleman topping Sandinista leader and former President Daniel Ortega by 49 percent to 38 percent.
The Sandinistas say the election was riddled with irregularities and have called for results to be annulled and new votes to be held in the departments (provinces) of Managua and Matagalpa.

Aleman has proclaimed himself president-elect and announced his cabinet. But Ortega has refused to concede defeat, saying he will wait until the Supreme Election Council (CSE) finishes reviewing the vote count.
The CSE has said it will release provisional results of the vote count on Thursday, converting the Friday protest into a potential powder keg if the results confirm the Sandinista defeat as expected.

Outside Sandinista headquarters, wearing a Che Guevara-style beret and the Sandinista red and black colours, activist Carlos Izaguirre said the party must defend itself against the "theft" of its victory by Liberal fraud.
"We must have massive protests to let them know they can't get away with this theft. In Nicaragua, if you don't yell you get crushed," he said.
